standard.title: Continuities and Changes in Australian Society Around 1900
standard.description: continuities and changes and their effects on ways of life and living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the development of colonial Australian society (AC9HH9K02), the effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians (AC9HH9K03), and the Federation movement (AC9HH9K04). They understand the founding conditions of Australian colonies and the political changes leading to Federation. They have not yet systematically examined the everyday living and working conditions of ordinary Australians around 1900, or the role of federal legislation in shaping those conditions.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine continuities and changes and their effects on ways of life, living conditions, political and legal institutions, and cultural expression around the turn of the 20th century in Australian society.

nodes.label: Living and working conditions around 1900 — comparison with 1800
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the main features of living and working conditions around 1900, including housing, sanitation, transport, education and industry, and compare these with conditions around 1800.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least two features of living or working conditions in Australia around 1900 and note one way they differed from conditions around 1800.
nodes.typical_width: Identify the main features of housing, sanitation, transport, education, agriculture and industry that influenced living and working conditions in Australia around 1900; compare these with conditions from early colonisation around 1800; examine differences between rural and urban settings using primary sources (photographs, paintings, diaries, newspapers).
wider: Examine the contrast between wealthy and working-class living conditions in a specific city (e.g. Sydney or Melbourne) around 1900 using photographs and newspaper sources — assessing how industrialisation created extreme inequality within cities
Compare living conditions for women in rural versus urban Australia around 1900, examining how gender, class, and geography intersected in shaping experience

Investigate conditions for First Nations Australians and non-European groups around 1900 — examining how their experiences of continuity and change differed fundamentally from those of European settlers
nodes.hinge_reason: The continuity/change comparison between 1800 and 1900 is the structural spine of this descriptor. Without a concrete picture of what conditions were like, students cannot analyse change meaningfully or evaluate the significance of reforms (Node 3).

response_modes.reason: Using multiple settings (rural vs urban, different social classes) prevents students from generalising from a single class or context. Primary sources are essential here — visual sources in particular make conditions tangible.

success_criteria: Identifies and describes at least three features of living or working conditions around 1900 (from different domains: housing, sanitation, transport, education, or industry)
Compares at least two of these features with conditions around 1800, identifying what changed and what remained continuous

nodes.label: Religious sectarianism and social division
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine the social and political impact of religious sectarianism between Catholics and Protestants in the formation of the Australian nation.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the religious divide between Catholics and Protestants in colonial Australia and explain one way it affected social or political life.
nodes.typical_width: Examine the social and political impact of religious sectarianism between Catholics and Protestants in colonial and early federal Australia, including how Irish Catholic identity intersected with social class, labour movements, and political allegiance; explain how sectarian tensions shaped community life and political divisions.
wider: Investigate how Irish Catholic identity in Australia created a distinctive social bloc with specific political loyalties, and trace this influence into early 20th century debates (e.g. conscription)
Examine how Protestant and Catholic communities established parallel educational and social institutions, and assess the long-term effects of this institutional division on Australian society

response_modes.reason: Connecting sectarianism to class, immigration (Irish background), and later political divisions (conscription debate, Labor Party) gives students a richer picture of how religious identity operated as a social and political force.

success_criteria: Describes the Catholic-Protestant divide in colonial and early federal Australia
Explains at least one way sectarian tensions shaped social or political life

nodes.label: Federal legislation and its effects on living and working conditions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how early federal laws (particularly the Harvester Judgement and social welfare legislation) affected working conditions and standards of living in Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one federal law or legal decision that affected working conditions or living standards, and describe its effect.
nodes.typical_width: Explain how federal legislation and legal decisions — especially the Harvester Judgement (1907, establishing the basic wage) and the introduction of pensions — affected working conditions and standards of living; connect these reforms to broader continuities and changes in Australian society around the turn of the 20th century.
wider: Investigate the Harvester Judgement in depth — examining the reasoning behind Justice Higgins' decision, what it established as a 'living wage', and how this concept of a minimum standard of living became embedded in Australian labour law
Compare the pace of labour reform in Australia with that in Britain or the United States — assessing whether Australia was genuinely progressive in labour rights or aligned with international trends

Examine the exclusions in early welfare legislation — who did not benefit from the basic wage or pension entitlements — and assess how these exclusions reflected the racial and gender assumptions of early federal policy

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the picture of conditions (Node 1) with institutional responses — legislation represents the political system responding to social change. Students should connect what conditions were like with why reforms were demanded and what they achieved.

success_criteria: Explains at least one specific federal law or legal decision and its effect on working or living conditions
Connects at least one legislative change to a broader continuity or change in Australian society around 1900
